intro:
This track is about keeping a copy of data close by, in memory, where a program can reach it in a fraction of a millisecond. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows, such as a barista's jug of milk on the counter, a post office clerk who serves one window at a time, or a Pay button pressed twice. Then they open up the machinery, with real measurements on your own laptop.

The worked example throughout is Redis, a program that holds data in a computer's memory and answers other programs' requests very fast. Valkey, a free copy of Redis that others have developed since 2024, comes up where it differs. So do numbers published by companies that run caches at huge scale, such as Meta, Twitter and Cloudflare.

By the end, you can:

- say why a small copy close by answers most requests, and what its misses cost the database behind it;
- follow how Redis runs every command in turn on one thread, and why one slow command makes everyone wait;
- pick the right type of value for a job, and count things in very little memory;
- say when an expired key really leaves memory, and what a full Redis does;
- choose how a cache is filled, and stop a hundred programs from rebuilding the same copy at once;
- keep a cache from serving an old value after a change;
- build a limit on attempts, and a record that turns a payment sent twice into one charge;
- say what survives a crash, and how a cluster splits the keys over several servers.

The ten lessons:

1. Why caches work: latency, locality and hit ratios
2. Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands
3. Core data types and their encodings
4. Bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo and the Redis 8 built-ins
5. Expiry, eviction and memory
6. Caching patterns and stampedes
7. Keeping a cache honest: invalidation, leases and consistency
8. Rate limiting and idempotency keys
9. Persistence and replication
10. Redis Cluster and production operations

You need to read a little code: every sample comes in Java and in Kotlin. You don't need to know anything about caches or Redis, because every term is explained the first time it appears. The first lesson needs no Redis at all. The second builds the picture the rest of the track uses: one thread runs every command to the end. A few ideas from the Operating systems track come back in lessons 9 and 10 (the page cache, copy-on-write and memory allocation), with a reminder each time. Some topics start here and finish later in the course: scripts and transactions in Transactions, locks in Faults, time and truth, copying and splitting data in Replication and Partitioning, and Redis's message streams in Messaging and logs.

The labs are in `labs/redis`, one package per lesson (`sfz.cache.l01` to `sfz.cache.l10`). Each lab is a set of failing tests: run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.lNN.*'` from the `labs` folder until it passes, and `./gradlew :redis:solutionTest` runs the same tests against the finished answers. Some labs model a mechanism in plain code, such as a small cache, an event loop, a counting sketch, a replication backlog or a cluster router, and need only a JDK, the kit that compiles and runs Java. The others start a real Redis 8.10.3 for the tests, so Docker must be running. Docker is a free program that runs small, separate Linux systems, called containers, on your computer. Try its use `env/redis.yml` (one server, plus a tiny one for eviction), `env/redis-ha.yml` (a primary, a replica and three Sentinels) and `env/redis-cluster.yml` (three cluster nodes). Everything was tested with Redis 8.10.3, Jedis 8.0.2, Lettuce 7.9.0, Testcontainers 2.0.5 and JDK 25, and lessons name the Redis version of every command newer than 7.2.
cheatsheet:
## Why caches work (lesson 1)

A cache is a copy of part of the data, kept somewhere faster to reach. Each rung of this ladder is ten to a thousand times slower than the one above:

| One read from | About |
|---|---|
| the processor's own L1 cache | 1 ns |
| RAM, the computer's working memory | 100 ns |
| a file the operating system already holds in memory | 1 µs |
| another machine in the same data center (a round trip) | 0.1 to 0.5 ms |
| a machine in another region of the world | 70 ms or more |

The hit ratio h is the share of lookups the cache answers. Average time = h × hit time + (1 − h) × miss time, and the slow layer behind the cache sees (1 − h) × requests. Going from 90% to 99% hits, or from 99% to 99.9%, cuts its load tenfold: count the misses, not the hits. A request with n lookups hits on all of them with probability h^n. A small cache catches most reads because popularity is skewed: with Zipf popularity at α = 1, the top 1% of a million keys get 68% of the requests. A miss-ratio curve says how big the cache must be. A cache is a copy, never the only copy.

## How Redis runs commands (lesson 2)

One thread runs every command to the end, one after another. So **every single command is atomic** (it happens completely or not at all, and nothing runs in the middle of it), and **one slow command stalls every client**. Background threads, forked children and I/O threads (`io-threads`, off by default) do side work and never run commands.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is one command atomic? | Yes, always. A sequence of commands is not. |
| What makes Redis slow for everyone? | One command whose work grows with the data (`KEYS`, `HGETALL` on a big hash, `DEL` of a big key, a long script), a fork, a starved machine. |
| A round trip or a command? | A `GET` costs about half a microsecond of server time and a few hundred microseconds of network. Send commands in batches. |

## Types and memory (lessons 3 and 4)

| Need | Type | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| A value, a counter | string: `SET`, `INCR` | a plain `SET` drops the TTL (time to live); add `KEEPTTL` |
| An object's fields | hash: `HSET`, `HINCRBY` | compact up to 512 fields of 64 bytes, then a hash table |
| A ranking | sorted set: `ZADD`, `ZRANGE ... REV` | ties sort by member; ranks start at 0; compact up to 128 members |
| Membership | set | `SMEMBERS` on a big set reads it all; use `SSCAN` |
| Cards active today | bitmap: `SETBIT`, `BITCOUNT` | needs a small, dense number for each card |
| How many different | HyperLogLog: `PFADD`, `PFCOUNT` | 12 KB, about 0.81% off, can't list its members |
| Card readers nearby | geo (a sorted set) | distances treat the Earth as a ball |
| A work queue or event log | stream | trim with `MAXLEN ~` or `MINID ~` |

Small hashes, sets and sorted sets are stored as listpacks, compact blocks of memory. Past the limits above, Redis converts them to bigger structures and never converts back: a 128-member sorted set took about 1 KB, a 129-member one about 11 KB. Every key also costs fixed bookkeeping: about 55 bytes for a tiny key on Redis 8.10, 46 on Valkey 9.1.

## Expiry and eviction (lesson 5)

| | Expiry | Eviction |
|---|---|---|
| Removes | keys whose deadline (TTL) has passed | keys Redis picks when `used_memory` reaches `maxmemory` |
| When | when a command touches the key, plus a clean-up round 10 times a second | before a write that needs room |
| Set with | `EXPIRE`, `SET ... EX`, `PERSIST` | `maxmemory`, `maxmemory-policy` |
| Default | no deadline | `maxmemory 0` (no limit) and `noeviction`: writes fail when memory is full |

Data you can't lose (payment records, rate limits, locks): `noeviction`, a TTL on every key and an alert near `maxmemory`. A cache: `allkeys-lru`. Keep the two in separate servers. The `volatile-*` policies act like `noeviction` when no key has a TTL.

Eviction is a bet on the future: LRU bets on recency, LFU on frequency, ARC and W-TinyLFU on both, and S3-FIFO and SIEVE drop one-hit wonders quickly and move nothing on a hit. Redis samples 5 keys into a pool of 16 and evicts the best candidate (LRU, LFU, or LRM, least recently modified, since 8.6).

## Caching patterns and stampedes (lesson 6)

| Pattern | Who loads on a miss | Who writes, and when |
|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside | your code | your code: the database first, then `DEL` the key |
| Read-through | the cache's loader | pair it with a write pattern |
| Write-through | | the cache, which writes the database before `put` returns |
| Write-behind | | the cache, now in memory and the database later (until it writes, the cache holds the only copy) |
| Refresh-ahead | the cache, before the deadline | |

For payments: cache-aside, `DEL` after the database has saved the change, a TTL on every entry with ±10% random jitter, and "not found" cached briefly. A stampede is many readers rebuilding the same expired key at once: 10 reads a second and a 3-second rebuild make 30 rebuilds.

| Stampede fix | Reach |
|---|---|
| single-flight (one load per key, the others wait for it: a `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures, Caffeine's `get(key, loader)`) | one program |
| `SET lock:<k> <token> NX PX 2000`, and the losers poll the cache | every server |
| XFetch: refresh early when `now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry` | every server, no lock; about 2 to 3 rebuilds per refresh at beta 1 |

## Keeping a cache honest (lesson 7)

A cache stays honest as long as no copy older than the newest delete can get into it.

| Way in | Fix |
|---|---|
| two writers' `SET`s arrive in the wrong order | delete instead of set, or set only if the version is newer |
| a slow reader read before the save and fills after the `DEL` (the stale set) | a lease: `SET lease:{k} <token> NX PX 10000` on a miss, the writer runs `DEL k lease:{k}`, and a Lua fill checks the token |
| a version check after a `DEL` or an eviction has nothing to compare with | leave a tombstone `{ver}` that outlives the slowest fill |
| the program dies between saving and `DEL` | take deletes from the database's own log of changes (CDC, change data capture), still through the version check |
| everything you haven't found | a TTL as the backstop, and a measured rate of wrong answers |

Meta's leases cut peak database load on stampede-prone keys from 17,000 to 1,300 queries a second, and measuring took its TAO cache from six to ten nines of consistency at five minutes.

## Rate limits and idempotency keys (lesson 8)

| Limiter | Kept per card or user | How exact |
|---|---|---|
| fixed window (`INCR` and a TTL in one script, or `INCREX ... EX 60 ENX` on 8.8) | one counter | up to twice the limit where two windows meet |
| sliding window log (a sorted set, one script) | one member per request | exact |
| sliding window counter | two counters | Cloudflare: 0.003% wrong decisions, 6% average deviation |
| token bucket (a hash of `tokens` and `ts`) | two numbers | a burst up to its size, then a steady rate |
| GCRA (one theoretical arrival time) | one number | the same answers as the token bucket |

An idempotency key makes a request sent twice count once. Claim it with `SET idem:<key> <pending> NX GET PX 30000` before the work; the pending value carries a fingerprint of the request and an owner token. After the work, store the exact response as DONE for 24 hours (`SET ... IFEQ <my pending>` on 8.4). PENDING with the same fingerprint: 409. A different fingerprint: 422. DONE: send the stored response again. A server that charges and dies before DONE still needs the payment provider's own idempotency key, or the database transaction.

## Surviving crashes (lesson 9)

| | The Redis process is killed (`kill -9`, out of memory) | The machine dies (power, kernel failure) | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| No persistence | everything | everything | none |
| RDB snapshots, default rules | writes since the last snapshot: minutes | the same | a fork, plus copies of the pages changed meanwhile |
| Append-only file, `everysec` (default) | nothing | about the last second | one `fsync()` a second, on a background thread |
| Append-only file, `always` | nothing | nothing | an `fsync()` every turn: far fewer writes a second |

`write()` puts bytes in the kernel's page cache in RAM; only `fsync()` waits until the disk holds them. A fork copies the page table on the main thread (48 MB for 24 GB of data; about 10 to 25 ms per GB on most machines, over 200 on some old cloud machines), and copy-on-write can nearly double memory under heavy writes. Turn off transparent huge pages.

Replication is asynchronous: a replica follows the stream of changes a little behind, and after a break catches up from the backlog (`repl-backlog-size`, 1 MB) or with a full snapshot. `WAIT n ms` counts the replicas that have this connection's writes and undoes nothing. `WAITAOF` (7.2) waits for `fsync()`.

| | Sentinel | Cluster |
|---|---|---|
| Data | one primary holds everything | split over primaries by hash slot |
| Failover | 3 or more Sentinels: a quorum agrees, a majority acts | the other primaries vote for a replica |
| Clients | ask a Sentinel where the primary is | load the slot table, follow `MOVED` and `ASK` |
| Commands with several keys | anything | only keys in one slot: use hash tags |

## Cluster (lesson 10)

`slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384`; when a key has a `{...}` with something inside, only that part is hashed. `MOVED <slot> <addr>`: the slot lives elsewhere, so update your table. `ASK <slot> <addr>`: the slot is moving, so send this one command there after `ASKING`. `CROSSSLOT`: a command, transaction or script names keys in more than one slot. Tag by the smallest unit that must change in one step (`{payment:p-981}`), never by shop or customer group.

## When Redis is slow (lesson 10)

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `SLOWLOG GET 10` | commands that ran over 10 ms on the command thread |
| `LATENCY LATEST`, `LATENCY DOCTOR` | forks, slow `fsync()` calls, long expiry rounds (set `latency-monitor-threshold` first) |
| `INFO commandstats` | calls and microseconds per command |
| `INFO persistence`, `INFO stats` | `latest_fork_usec`, `rdb_last_cow_size`, `evicted_keys`, `expired_keys` |
| `INFO memory` | `used_memory`, `used_memory_rss`, `mem_fragmentation_ratio` |
| `redis-cli --bigkeys`, `--memkeys`, `HOTKEYS` (8.6) | big keys and hot keys |
| `redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 100` | stalls of the machine itself |

Never `KEYS` on a busy server: `SCAN` with `MATCH` and `COUNT`. `UNLINK`, not `DEL`, for big keys.

## Java and Kotlin

Jedis and Lettuce are the two main Redis libraries for Java and Kotlin.

| | Jedis 8 | Lettuce 7.9 |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | `RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort(h, p).build()` | `RedisClient.create("redis://h:p")`, then `connect()` |
| Connections | a pool: one connection per call | one connection shared by all callers |
| Style | blocking calls | sync, async, reactive, Kotlin coroutines (`coroutines()`) |
| Pipelines and WAIT | `redis.pipelined()`: one connection for the batch | every call on the shared connection |
| Cluster | `RedisClusterClient` | `io.lettuce.core.cluster.RedisClusterClient` |
| Sentinel | `RedisSentinelClient` | `RedisURI.Builder.sentinel(...)` |

## Commands by version

| Since | Commands |
|---|---|
| 7.0 | functions (`FUNCTION LOAD`, `FCALL`), the multi-part append-only file, `EXPIRE ... NX/XX/GT/LT`, sharded pub/sub |
| 7.2 | `WAITAOF` |
| 7.4 | `HEXPIRE` and the other deadlines for single hash fields |
| 8.4 | `SET ... IFEQ`, `DELEX`, `XREADGROUP ... CLAIM`, `CLUSTER MIGRATION` |
| 8.6 | `XADD ... IDMP`, LRM eviction, `HOTKEYS` |
| 8.8 | `INCREX`, `XNACK` |
| 8.10 | `BACKUP` |

Valkey (BSD license, started from Redis 7.2.4 in 2024) runs everything up to 7.2; check the newer commands before you rely on them there.

## Where the rest went

MULTI, WATCH, pipelines and Lua in full: the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution. Locks, leases and fencing tokens: the Faults, time and truth track. Pub/sub and Streams: the Messaging and logs track's lesson on Redis. Copying and splitting data in general: the Replication and Partitioning tracks.
recap: A cache works because a few keys get most of the reads, and the slow layer behind it is a hundred to a thousand times slower. Count the misses: going from 99% to 99.9% hits cuts the database's load tenfold.
A store that lives in memory is fast mainly because it keeps data in plain structures. Redis runs every command on one thread, so each command is atomic, and one slow command stalls every client.

Memory goes per key and per type: compact listpacks up to a size limit, then hash tables and skip lists that never shrink back. Sketches such as HyperLogLog trade a known error for a fixed, small size.

Expiry removes keys whose deadline has passed, when they're touched and in sampled rounds. Eviction is a bet on which keys won't be needed again; data you can't lose gets `noeviction`, a cache `allkeys-lru`.
Caching patterns differ in who loads and who writes. For payments, use cache-aside: delete after saving, add jitter to deadlines, and stop stampedes with single-flight, a lock or XFetch.

Delete-on-write still loses to a slow reader that fills after the delete. A lease or a version check with tombstones makes Redis refuse the old copy, the database's change log covers crashed writers, and the TTL is the backstop.

Rate limits and idempotency keys check and record in one command or script. Pick fixed window, sliding log, sliding counter, token bucket or GCRA by how exact it must be and how much memory it may use.

Snapshots lose minutes; the append-only file with `everysec` loses nothing when only Redis dies and about a second when the machine does. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose a few seconds of answered writes.
Redis Cluster spreads keys over 16,384 slots. Clients route by slot and follow MOVED and ASK, and commands with several keys need one slot, which hash tags provide.
When Redis is slow, look for one slow command first (the slow log, the latency monitor, commandstats), then forks, big and hot keys, and the machine itself. SCAN, never KEYS; UNLINK for big keys.

quiz.q: A cache in front of a database answers 99% of 100,000 reads a second, with hits at 0.5 ms and misses at 10 ms. A change lifts the hit ratio to 99.9%. What happens?
options: The load on the database falls by 0.9%, and so does the average time per read
The load on the database falls from 1,000 to 100 queries a second, while the average time barely moves, from about 0.6 to 0.51 ms
Both the load and the time halve
Nothing measurable: past 99% a cache can't do better
quiz.why: The database sees only the misses: 1% of 100,000 is 1,000 a second, and 0.1% is 100. The average is 0.99 × 0.5 + 0.01 × 10 ≈ 0.6 ms before and 0.999 × 0.5 + 0.001 × 10 ≈ 0.51 ms after, because hits already make up almost all of it (lesson 1). Near the top, each extra nine is worth little in time and a tenfold cut in the database's load.

quiz.q: A clean-up job runs `KEYS fraud:*` over 30 million keys on a busy Redis. Another program sends `GET payment:42` meanwhile. What happens to the GET?
options: It runs at once on an I/O thread
It returns the value from before the KEYS started, like a snapshot
It fails at once with a BUSY error
It waits until the KEYS has walked every key, because one thread runs every command in turn
quiz.why: One thread runs every command to the end (lesson 2), so the GET waits in line behind a command that walks 30 million keys. I/O threads only read requests and write replies; they never run commands. BUSY is for scripts that run past 5 seconds, and Redis has no snapshot reads. SCAN does the same walk in small slices, so other clients are served in between (lesson 10).

quiz.q: A sorted set for each shop grows from 120 to 140 members, and `MEMORY USAGE` on it jumps about tenfold. Why?
options: Past 128 members (`zset-max-listpack-entries`) Redis converts the compact listpack into a skip list plus a hash table, and never converts back
The members got longer
The sorted set was copied for a snapshot
The scores became decimal numbers
quiz.why: Small sorted sets live in a listpack, one compact block of memory. At 129 members, or one member over 64 bytes, Redis converts the key to a skip list and a hash table, with pointers and headers for every member: about 1 KB became 11 KB on the lab server (lesson 3). Scores are always floating-point numbers, and a snapshot doesn't change how a key is stored.

quiz.q: You must count the different cards that paid at each shop each day, about 10 million cards in all, within about 1%, in as little memory as possible. Which structure?
options: A set of card ids per shop per day
A sorted set scored by time
A HyperLogLog per shop per day: at most 12 KB each, about 0.81% off
A hash from card id to count
quiz.why: A HyperLogLog estimates how many different items it has seen in at most 12 KB, whatever the count, usually within 0.81%, and `PFMERGE` combines several days (lesson 4). A set or a hash stores every id, hundreds of megabytes at this scale. The price: a HyperLogLog can't list or remove its members.

quiz.q: A Redis that holds idempotency keys runs with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`. When memory runs short, a 23-hour-old key disappears although its TTL was 24 hours, and a retried payment is charged twice. What removed it?
options: Expiry: Redis expires keys early when memory is tight
A replica deleted it
The expiry clean-up round picked it by mistake
Eviction: allkeys-lru picked the key that had gone unread longest, whatever its TTL
quiz.why: Expiry only removes keys whose deadline has passed, never early. Eviction removes keys Redis chooses when `used_memory` reaches `maxmemory`, and under allkeys-lru the key unread longest goes first: a 23-hour-old idempotency key is the perfect candidate (lesson 5). Data like this belongs on a server with `noeviction`, a `maxmemory` and an alert.

quiz.q: A popular shop's key is read about 10 times a second and takes 3 seconds to rebuild. About how many rebuilds start when it expires with a plain TTL, and with probabilistic early expiration (XFetch, beta = 1)?
options: 1 with a plain TTL, because the first miss rebuilds it, and 1 with XFetch
10 and 0: XFetch never lets the key expire
About 30 with a plain TTL, and about 2 or 3 with XFetch, starting a little before the deadline
About 30 with both: XFetch changes only when the rebuilds happen
quiz.why: Every read that arrives before the first rebuild finishes misses and rebuilds too: 10 a second × 3 seconds ≈ 30. XFetch lets each reader refresh early, with odds that rise near the deadline, so usually one or two readers refresh before it and nobody misses. The lesson's simulation measured 2.7 rebuilds per refresh, close to the paper's 2.4 (lesson 6).

quiz.q: A program saves a shop's new name in the database and then runs `DEL merchant:{m-17}`, yet readers keep getting the old name for an hour. Which race explains it, and what stops it?
options: Two writers' SETs arrived in the wrong order; delete instead of set
A reader read the old row before the save and stored it after the delete; fill only while a lease the delete removes is still valid, or only if the version is newer than any the cache has seen
Redis ignored the DEL because the key had a TTL; use PERSIST first
The DEL went to a replica; send it to the primary
quiz.why: The program already deletes, so SETs in the wrong order can't be the cause. This is the stale set: the DEL hit an empty key, then a slow reader's SET stored the row it had read before the save, with a full TTL (lesson 7). A lease taken on the miss and removed by the DEL makes the late fill fail, and a version check with a tombstone refuses it too. A TTL never blocks a DEL, and replicas refuse writes.

quiz.q: A rate limiter runs `INCR rl:card:7` and, if the result is 1, `EXPIRE rl:card:7 60`. The server running the limiter is killed between the two calls. What happens, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing: Redis runs both commands as one step because they come from the same client
The counter has no TTL and never resets, so the card stays blocked; do both in one Lua script, or `INCREX ... EX 60 ENX` on Redis 8.8
Redis notices the missing EXPIRE and sets a default TTL
The INCR is undone when the connection drops
quiz.why: Each command is atomic because one thread runs it to the end (lesson 2), but two commands are two steps, and a crash can fall between them (lesson 8). Nothing in Redis ties the INCR to the EXPIRE that should follow, and nothing is undone. A script runs the count and the deadline as one command, and Redis 8.8's INCREX does both in one built-in command.

quiz.q: The machine running Redis loses power. Which setting loses fewer writes that Redis had answered OK, and roughly how many?
options: RDB snapshots with the default rules: nothing, since snapshots are on disk
They lose the same: both write to disk
The append-only file with everysec: about the last second. RDB loses everything since the last snapshot, often minutes
The append-only file with everysec: nothing, since every write is logged before the reply
quiz.why: A snapshot holds the data as it was at its fork, and with the default rules that can be minutes old (lesson 9). The append-only file hands every write to the kernel before Redis answers, which protects against a crash of the Redis process. But a power cut also wipes the kernel's page cache, so writes not yet passed through `fsync()` are lost: about one second under everysec. Only `always` loses nothing, at a large cost in speed.

quiz.q: The idempotency store will need 300 GB and 1 million commands a second, far more than one server can take. Sentinel or Cluster?
options: Cluster: it splits the keys over many primaries by hash slot, each with its own replica and failover
Sentinel: it adds servers when memory runs low
Sentinel with more replicas, reading from all of them
Either: they are two names for the same thing
quiz.why: Sentinel watches one primary that holds every key and promotes a replica when it fails. Replicas copy everything, so they split neither the memory nor the writes (lessons 9 and 10). A cluster gives each primary a share of the 16,384 slots and fails each one over on its own. The price: commands with several keys, transactions and scripts need their keys in one slot.
